title: Best Shower Curtains 2026: Mold & Wash Comparison
description: iDesign PEVA, Maytex fabric, Gorilla Grip, Threshold and West Elm organic cotton — compared on drying speed, machine washability, weighted hems and whether each one still needs a liner.
lede: The $79 organic cotton curtain looks beautiful, and owner reviews keep describing mold on its lower hem within weeks — because nobody told them it needed a liner underneath.
methodology: This comparison is desk research. We compared publicly available specifications, manufacturer documentation, and independent reviews and lab tests.

sections.heading: The most important thing to understand first
paragraphs: Most people confuse decorative curtains and functional liners. They are different products doing different jobs. A decorative curtain (fabric, cotton, linen) provides privacy and visual appeal but is not waterproof — it faces the room, not the shower spray. A liner (PEVA, polyester) is waterproof, faces the shower, and keeps water off the floor. Most setups need both.

The West Elm organic cotton curtain draws its worst reviews from buyers who hung it alone without a liner; they describe mold at the hem within weeks. That is not a product failure — it is a category misunderstanding. Conversely, the iDesign PEVA liner is purely functional: it will never look beautiful, but non-porous PEVA gives mold almost nothing to work with and it costs $8. Understanding which one you actually need determines which product is right for you.

sections.heading: How we compared
paragraphs: The comparison assumes the setup most bathrooms actually have: a main bathroom in daily use by two people, with an exhaust fan, PEVA and polyester liners on the inner rod and fabric curtains on the outer.

Machine wash durability is read from each manufacturer's care instructions — recommended cycle, water temperature and drying method — alongside what long-term owner reviews say about shrinkage, hem condition and color or pattern fading after repeated washing.

sections.heading: How we picked
paragraphs: We compared: mold resistance as a function of material and drying speed, machine washability under each manufacturer's stated care instructions, whether a weighted hem genuinely prevents billowing, water repellency, and value relative to the functional job each product does. Price ranged from $8 to $89.

No-name PEVA liners under $5 with no grommet reinforcement are excluded — cracked grommets within a month are the dominant complaint in their reviews. Shower curtain rings and rods are also excluded as separate categories.

sections.heading: Comparison table
paragraphs: Key published specifications across all five products. Mold resistance summarises how the material behaves — non-porous plastics shed water fastest, untreated natural fibres slowest. Billowing is yes/no for the liner floating into the tub. Machine wash follows each manufacturer's stated care instructions.

| Product | Price | Material | Mold Resistance | Billowing | Machine Wash |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iDesign PEVA Liner | $8–12 | 100% PEVA | High — non-porous, dries fast | Yes | No — wipe clean |
| Maytex Smart Curtain | $18–25 | 100% Polyester | Good — antimicrobial finish | Yes | Yes — cold, gentle |
| Gorilla Grip Liner | $20–25 | Heavy PEVA (0.15mm) | High — non-porous, dries fast | No | No — wipe clean |
| Threshold Curtain | $22–35 | Poly/Cotton | Moderate — blend holds moisture | Yes | Yes — cold, gentle |
| West Elm Organic Cotton | $59–89 | GOTS Cotton | Low without a liner — untreated fibre | Yes | Yes — cold, gentle |

The Gorilla Grip is the only product here that eliminates billowing — the weighted magnets at the hem seal against the tub floor. The West Elm's low mold resistance assumes use without a liner; with a liner underneath it would not contact water directly and mold would not be an issue. The iDesign and Gorilla Grip are functional liners only; the others serve as decorative curtains that also have some functional properties.

sections.heading: iDesign PEVA Shower Curtain Liner
paragraphs: At $8–12 this is the budget baseline. PEVA is polyethylene vinyl acetate — the non-chlorinated alternative to PVC that skips the plasticizer off-gassing associated with the chemical smell of older vinyl liners. It hangs flat, repels water on contact, and dries within about 20 minutes of the shower ending — which is why mold barely features in its reviews. Mold needs sustained moisture. PEVA denies it.

The rust-proof grommets are the part owners praise most — cracking and metal staining at the liner edge, the dominant failure mode in cheaper liners, rarely come up in its reviews. The limitation is physics: without weight at the hem, the liner drifts into the tub in most showers. It's not uncomfortable, but it touches your legs. For anyone who finds that annoying, the Gorilla Grip liner fixes it for $12 more. The iDesign is purely functional — it will never look like anything — but at $8 it is the best argument that mold prevention does not require spending more.

sections.heading: Maytex Smart Curtains Fabric Shower Curtain
paragraphs: A 100% polyester curtain with an antimicrobial treatment that covers both decorative and functional roles without requiring a separate liner. Owners who use it without a liner report the antimicrobial finish holds up well — the recurring complaint is minor discoloration at the very bottom hem corner where it contacts pooling tub water, rather than active mold growth.

Machine washing is what it is built for: the care label calls for cold on gentle, and long-term reviews describe no meaningful shrinkage, no fraying at the hem, and color that holds without significant fading. Polyester dries faster than cotton after washing, which matters for weekly cleaning routines. At $18–25 it sits in a good middle position — you get a curtain that looks like fabric, avoids the plastic-liner look, and can handle weekly machine washing without degrading. The billowing issue is the same as the iDesign: no weighted hem, no seal.

sections.heading: Gorilla Grip Original Shower Curtain Liner
paragraphs: The weighted magnets along the hem are the single most tangible upgrade available in a shower liner at any price point. Owners consistently report that the hem stays put and the liner does not billow into the tub. The heavy-gauge PEVA (0.15mm vs the iDesign's thinner gauge) also hangs with more body — it drapes rather than clings — and at $20–25 it costs only $12–15 more than the iDesign.

Mold resistance is the same story as the iDesign. PEVA dries fast regardless of gauge, and owners report the heavier material holds its shape without sagging or bunching at the grommets over months of daily use. The mold-resistant manufacturing claim is accurate in the sense that PEVA is inherently inhospitable to mold — but the real protection is drying speed, not a chemical treatment. This is the liner to buy if you care about the liner staying inside the tub.

sections.heading: Threshold Fabric Shower Curtain
paragraphs: Target's house brand delivers genuine value in the pattern variety that PEVA liners cannot: florals, stripes, geometric prints, solids — and it changes with each season. The poly-cotton blend is machine washable, holds its color through repeated washing according to long-term reviews, and is sold at a price that makes replacing it annually for a seasonal refresh feel reasonable rather than wasteful.

The mold rating is honest: poly-cotton blends absorb more moisture than pure polyester and take longer to dry, which means the bottom 4–6 inches of the curtain stay damp for longer after each shower. Owners who hang it without a liner describe light discoloration at the tub-level hem after a few months — not alarming mold growth, but visible. The solution is straightforward: use it as a decorative curtain with a PEVA liner behind it, as intended. Without a liner, mold develops faster on cotton-blend curtains than on polyester. At $22–35 for the range of patterns available, it is one of the better pattern-versus-price ratios in mass-market shower curtains.

sections.heading: West Elm Organic Cotton Shower Curtain
paragraphs: GOTS-certified organic cotton at $59–89 is a legitimate material claim — the Global Organic Textile Standard certification covers the entire supply chain, not just the fiber source. The natural texture is visually distinct from synthetic curtains in a way that photographs well and matches a bathroom designed around natural materials. It is machine washable cold on gentle, and owners report the weave holds its shape and size through repeated washing.

The mold complaints it draws are a use-case error: the curtain gets hung without a liner, and organic cotton, being an untreated natural fibre, absorbs shower humidity and stays damp for hours. Owners describe mould at the hem within a couple of months. With a proper PEVA liner behind it, the West Elm curtain never contacts shower spray directly and the mold issue does not arise. But that adds $8–12 in liner cost and requires a double-rod setup. For anyone building a premium bathroom with that setup in mind, the organic cotton is worth the price. For anyone who wants one curtain that does everything, it is not the right product.

faqs.q: Do I need both a curtain and a liner, or just one?
faqs.a: Most shower setups benefit from both — a functional liner (PEVA or polyester) on the inside that contacts water, and a decorative curtain on the outside facing the bathroom. The liner handles water control and mold resistance. The curtain handles aesthetics. Single-curtain setups work fine with fabric curtains that have antimicrobial treatment (like the Maytex) or are made from quick-drying polyester. Organic cotton and cotton-blend curtains without a liner will mold at the hem within weeks to months.

faqs.q: How do weighted hem magnets actually work?
faqs.a: The magnets are embedded in small weights sewn into the bottom hem of the liner, spaced every few inches. They attract to a metal tub or are heavy enough to prevent the lightweight PEVA from floating. In a jetted tub or a shower with strong spray pressure, the magnets add enough downward force to keep the hem against the tub floor. The Gorilla Grip uses this design, and a hem that stays down is the thing its reviews mention most. On acrylic or fiberglass tubs without ferrous metal content, the magnetic attraction is weaker, but the weight alone still reduces billowing significantly.

faqs.q: Why does PEVA resist mold better than fabric?
faqs.a: Mold growth requires sustained moisture. PEVA is a non-porous plastic that releases water quickly and dries within 20–30 minutes of shower end. Fabric — especially natural fibers like cotton — absorbs water into the material and stays damp for 2–4 hours. That extended dampness is exactly what mold needs to establish. Antimicrobial-treated polyester reduces but does not eliminate this: the treatment slows mold colonization, but fabric still holds moisture longer than plastic. Drying speed, not chemical treatment, is the primary mold-resistance mechanism.

faqs.q: How often should I wash or replace my shower liner?
faqs.a: PEVA liners should be wiped down monthly with a damp cloth and a mild cleaning spray — they are not designed for machine washing and the heat can warp the material. Replace when you see pink or black growth that won't wipe off, typically every 6–12 months at the $8–25 price point. Fabric curtains can be machine washed cold on gentle weekly or bi-weekly and should be replaced when the hem frays or antimicrobial treatment loses effectiveness, usually after 1–2 years.

faqs.q: Is PEVA safe? I've heard concerns about shower liner chemicals.
faqs.a: PEVA (polyethylene vinyl acetate) is PVC-free and does not contain phthalate plasticizers, which are the primary concern with older vinyl shower curtains. That new shower curtain smell associated with PVC liners comes from plasticizer off-gassing. PEVA does have a mild initial smell that dissipates within a day or two of hanging. It is widely considered a safer alternative to PVC for indoor household use and is the standard material in EPA-friendly product guidelines for shower liners.

faqs.q: What does GOTS certification actually mean for a shower curtain?
faqs.a: The Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS) certification verifies that the fiber is organically grown (no synthetic pesticides or fertilizers) and that the manufacturing process meets environmental and social criteria throughout the supply chain. For a shower curtain, it means the cotton is pesticide-free at source and the dyes and finishing chemicals meet restricted substance standards. It does not confer any mold resistance, waterproofing, or functional shower performance benefit — it is a material sourcing and manufacturing claim, not a performance claim.

faqs.q: Can I use a fabric curtain in a walk-in shower with no tub?
faqs.a: Yes, but the setup matters. Walk-in showers without a tub lip have no surface for liner magnets to seal against — billowing is less of an issue because there is no enclosed tub space creating suction. However, a decorative fabric curtain in a walk-in shower without a liner will get direct spray contact, accelerating mold growth. Use a separate PEVA liner hung on an inner rod, or choose a quick-drying antimicrobial polyester curtain like the Maytex that can handle light spray contact without mold developing within weeks.

offerNotes.idesign-peva-shower-curtain-liner: Best budget liner — $8, PVC-free PEVA that dries in about 20 minutes so mold gets no foothold. Billows without a weighted hem.
offerNotes.maytex-fabric-shower-curtain: Best mid-range fabric — antimicrobial polyester, machine washable cold on gentle, no separate liner required.
offerNotes.gorilla-grip-shower-liner: Best liner overall — weighted hem magnets eliminate billowing, heavy-gauge PEVA, fast-drying and mold-resistant by material.
offerNotes.threshold-fabric-shower-curtain: Best pattern variety — poly-cotton blend, seasonal prints, machine washable. Pair with a PEVA liner for best mold resistance.
offerNotes.west-elm-organic-cotton-shower-curtain: Best premium aesthetic — GOTS organic cotton, machine washable with no shrinkage reported by owners. Requires a separate liner; not for use alone.

pinDescription: Owners report the $79 organic cotton curtain molds at the hem — because it needs a liner underneath.

products.review: The baseline that holds up. Mold barely features in its reviews because PEVA dries in about 20 minutes — not because of any chemical treatment. Rust-proof grommets are what owners say survive longest. The one functional gap is billowing: no weight at the hem means the liner floats into the tub in most showers. For $8, the mold performance is hard to argue with. For billowing control, spend the extra $12 on the Gorilla Grip.
pros: Non-porous PEVA dries in about 20 minutes, denying mold the moisture it needs
PVC-free PEVA — no phthalate plasticizers or off-gassing smell after day one
Rust-proof grommets — cracking and staining rarely come up in owner reviews
cons: Billows into the tub in most showers — no weighted hem to seal against the tub floor
Purely functional — no aesthetic value, not a decorative curtain replacement

products.review: The best single-product solution for anyone who wants a fabric look without buying a separate liner. Antimicrobial polyester is the reason mold complaints are rare — where owners do report an issue it is minor hem discoloration, not active growth. Repeated cold/gentle washing leaves the color and hem intact according to long-term reviews. Polyester dries faster than cotton after washing, which matters if you're washing weekly. The billowing issue is shared with the iDesign — no weighted hem — but as a decorative curtain rather than a liner, it's less of a functional problem.
pros: Antimicrobial treatment — the fewest mould complaints of the liners here
Machine washable cold on gentle — owners report no shrinkage, no hem fraying, good color retention
Polyester dries faster than cotton after washing — important for weekly cleaning
cons: No weighted hem — billows like any unweighted curtain in high-spray showers
Antimicrobial treatment effectiveness diminishes with repeated hot washing — use cold

products.review: The weighted magnets along the hem are not a marketing claim — owner reviews return to them constantly, and a hem that stays against the tub floor is the most cited reason people repurchase it. The heavier 0.15mm PEVA gauge drapes with more body than standard liners and holds its position. Mold resistance is the same as the iDesign, because PEVA dries quickly regardless of thickness. At $20–25, it costs $12–17 more than the iDesign for two meaningful upgrades: no billowing, and a stiffer hang. If the liner touching your legs bothers you, this is the fix.
pros: Weighted hem magnets — owners consistently report the liner stays inside the tub
Heavy-gauge 0.15mm PEVA drapes with more body and holds position better than thin liners
Same fast-drying, mold-resistant PEVA as the iDesign at double the gauge
cons: Still purely functional — no decorative value as a standalone curtain
Magnetic attachment is weaker on acrylic/fiberglass tubs vs. cast iron or steel

products.review: The honest version of the Target house-brand pitch: the pattern selection is genuinely excellent and changes seasonally, which makes refreshing a bathroom for $25–35 reasonable. The poly-cotton blend washes well — reviews describe good color retention and no hem fraying over repeated cycles. The mold caveat is real — poly-cotton holds moisture longer than pure polyester, and owners who hang it without a liner describe light discoloration at the tub-level hem within a few months. Pair it with the Gorilla Grip liner behind it and the mold issue disappears entirely, which is how fabric curtains are designed to be used.
pros: Seasonal pattern variety at $22–35 — the widest design selection at this price
Holds colour through repeated washing with no hem fraying
Poly-cotton blend feels more substantial than pure polyester curtains
cons: Poly-cotton retains moisture longer than polyester — mold develops faster when used without a liner
Requires a separate PEVA liner for proper mold protection, adding $8–25 to total cost

products.review: The GOTS certification is real and the organic cotton texture is visually distinct from anything synthetic in this comparison — it photographs well, and owners report the weave holds through repeated machine washing without shrinkage. Mold is the weakest point of any curtain here, but that is a use-case problem, not a product defect. Organic cotton is untreated and hygroscopic — hung alone in a shower, it absorbs humidity, and reviews describe mold colonising the hem within weeks. Hung as the outer decorative curtain with a PEVA liner behind it, the organic cotton never contacts shower spray and performs beautifully. The total cost with a liner is $70–100, which is a legitimate premium for a bathroom that earns it.
pros: GOTS-certified organic cotton — genuine supply chain certification, not a marketing label
Natural texture is visually distinct from synthetic curtains, photos exceptionally well
No shrinkage reported through repeated washing; weave stays intact
cons: Owners report mold at the hem within weeks when used without a liner — not rated for standalone shower use
Requires separate PEVA liner to function correctly — adds $8–25 and a double-rod setup
Premium price for aesthetics only; no functional performance advantage over polyester

recommendedFor.label: For mold prevention on a budget
recommendedFor.reason: Renters or households who want reliable mold resistance with minimal spending — $8 PEVA dries in about 20 minutes and mold rarely appears in its reviews.

recommendedFor.label: For a single-curtain setup without a liner
recommendedFor.reason: Households that want fabric aesthetics without managing a double-rod setup — antimicrobial polyester handles both the look and basic mold resistance.

recommendedFor.label: For anyone annoyed by a liner billowing into the tub
recommendedFor.reason: The weighted hem magnets solve billowing definitively — the best functional upgrade available in a shower liner for $20–25.

recommendedFor.label: For decorating on a seasonal budget
recommendedFor.reason: Bathrooms where switching curtains seasonally makes sense — the pattern variety and machine-washability make it the best value decorative curtain.

recommendedFor.label: For a premium natural-material bathroom
recommendedFor.reason: Bathrooms already designed around organic or natural materials, with a double-rod setup and a PEVA liner already in place — the aesthetic payoff is real when used correctly.
